extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, and critics of literature and art history interested in classical/Hellenic aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying classical (Hellenic) aesthetic standards for creating or evaluating art and literature—how form, medium, temperament, and cultural conditions produce the 'Hellenic ideal'. Useful for creative writers or artists seeking classical clarity, repose, and generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic immersion in the tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: “no one had, if I may say so, made himself a pagan for the purpose of penetrating antiquity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To penetrate antiquity (or a classical tradition) one must internalize it, not merely consult it like a book. Genuine enthusiasm and personal assimilation of the tradition are required rather than second-hand, purely scholarly acquaintance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthusiasm as a source of divinatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: “Enthusiasm... was the secret of his divinatory power over the Hellenic world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual insight into a tradition is reinforced by temperament and bodily excitement: fervent personal feeling, friendships, and a responsive temperament can deepen aesthetic perception and creative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated sensibility for art's beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “The beauty of art demands a higher sensibility than the beauty of nature... the beauty of art... must be awakened and repaired by culture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste for art needs cultivation (education, practice, youthful training). Natural appreciation alone is insufficient; creators and audiences should develop cultural habits and training to perceive artistic beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of form and motive (avoid mere symbolism)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Venus of Melos: it is “in no sense a symbol... The mind begins and ends with the finite image, yet loses no part of the spiritual motive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for artworks in which the sensuous form fully embodies the spiritual or intellectual motive—form and meaning should be saturated and identical, not merely suggestive or allegorical placeholders for ideas beyond the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of sensuous form to its matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Medieval/oriental works often present forms that are “inadequate to the matter they clothe”; forms should not merely hint at what they cannot express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose forms and modes of expression that can actually carry the subject-matter. Avoid using modes that only symbolically point to an idea the form cannot sensibly render.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match medium to the imaginative motive
rubrics_metrics.description: “Architecture... deals when the thoughts of man concerning himself are still indistinct... Painting, music, and poetry... are the special arts of the romantic and modern ages... sculpture... deals immediately with man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the artistic medium that best suits the motive: sculpture for the human type and pure form, painting and poetry for situations and inward complexity, architecture for monumental/practical projection. Do not expect one medium to do what another is best suited to achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural limitations are a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture “renounces the power of expression by sinking or heightening tones... limitation of its resources is part of its pride.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sculpture (and similar formal arts) embrace constraints—purity of form, limited colour, absence of background—to reveal the ideal. Limitations (no atmospheric modulation, little colour) sharpen the medium's expressive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heiterkeit (blitheness/repose) and Allgemeinheit (generality/breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Heiterkeit--blitheness or repose, and Allgemeinheit--generality or breadth, are, then, the supreme characteristics of the Hellenic ideal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for serene repose and a broad, generalizing vision in the classical mode: avoid frantic intensity or excessive particularity. This breadth is the product of minute, severe culture, not laxity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purge accidental detail to reveal types
rubrics_metrics.description: Art “abstracts from [detail]... All that is accidental... it gradually purges away.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on essential, archetypal features rather than ephemeral particularities. Abstracting away accidental details produces clearer, more powerful representations of character or form (especially important in sculpture and classical composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control the intensity of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellenic law “keeps passion always below that degree of intensity at which it must necessarily be transitory, never winding up the features to one note of anger, or desire, or surprise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain moderated emotion in style and depiction; avoid single-note extremes or grotesque exaggerations that render a work transient or caricatural rather than timeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize both temporal conditions and enduring standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “The artist is the child of his time... but besides these conditions of time and place... there is also an element of permanence, a standard of taste.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or create with awareness of historical/contextual influences while also appealing to enduring standards of taste transmitted through tradition. Balance contemporaneity with canonical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/social origins of an artistic ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek ideals arose from social practices: the palaestra, contests for beauty, gymnastic and religious rituals (beauty becoming a civic distinction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and, when appropriate, evoke the social practices and rituals that undergird an aesthetic ideal—collective valuation and institutions (rituals, contests, education) help shape and maintain an artistic standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive inwardness or mysticism in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle-age and oriental art often struggle because forms are “only the symbol or type of an inexpressible world... forms of sense struggle vainly with it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make forms merely vessels for inaccessible mystic content; keep thought and sensuous form at comparable levels so that the work’s outward embodiment can adequately carry its inward meaning.
